comments.author: Kuanze Ma
comments.comment: The hard part is less the router API and more the eval contract around it. If two harnesses solve the same task with different tool traces, you need task-level success checks, cost, latency, and failure taxonomy in one schema, or the cheapest route can quietly optimize for broken work.

comments.author: Philip Z. Borge
comments.comment: The part teams underestimate is calibration drift: a router that was optimal last month can quietly become expensive or wrong after one model update. I’d rather see firms evaluate by workflow failure modes, not leaderboard rank - extraction accuracy, citation faithfulness, tool-call recovery, and escalation rate. What’s your minimum eval set size before trusting a new model in production routing?

comments.author: Jeff Prestes (雷悟)
comments.comment: The hard part is not giving an agent wallet access, it is making the custody layer the final authority. I like treating the LLM as a proposer only: it can draft an action, but limits, quorum, allowlists, velocity caps, and human review decide whether anything moves. What failure mode do you test first - bad prompt, compromised credential, or valid action at the wrong time? #AI

comments.author: CA Ankur Sharma
comments.comment: Multi-agent governance gets real only when traces, evals, and API policy live in the same review loop. Otherwise teams end up debugging agent behavior after the blast radius is already visible. Curious if the sessions will cover how to define ownership when one agent’s output becomes another agent’s input.

comments.author: Przemek Tomczak, CPA, CA, CISA
comments.comment: The token reduction example is the part most teams should study: tool selection is often a retrieval problem before it is an agent problem. In production, I’ve seen evals become useful when they test “allowed but wrong” actions, not just pass/fail task completion. How are people here separating policy violations from operationally bad decisions in their eval suites? #AgenticAI

comments.author: Vladyslav Nyzhashchyy 🦫
comments.comment: 290,000 possible paths is exactly where voice agents stop being demo problems and start becoming state-management problems. The useful pattern I’ve seen is to treat the LLM as the language layer, but keep routing, retries, tool eligibility, and handoff criteria as explicit control logic. Curious how much of that pipeline was deterministic vs model-decided?
